explanations.explanation: Three it is, friend. Abraham looks up and sees three men standing nearby (Genesis 18:2). That's quite a crowd to show up at one tent in the heat of the day. Hold on to that number, because Abraham is about to get very busy.

Close, but the text counts one more. Genesis 18:2 says Abraham saw three men standing nearby. Two would have been a lighter afternoon for him. Three means more people to look after, and he's about to take that seriously.

Seven would be a whole lot of company, friend. The text says Abraham saw three men standing nearby (Genesis 18:2). Seven would have been a tent full of surprise guests. Three is plenty to get him moving.

True! He was sitting at the entrance of his tent in the heat of the day (Genesis 18:1). Then he spots three men, and he runs to meet them and bows low to the ground (Genesis 18:2). Sitting to sprinting, just like that. I get winded reaching for a cooling rack, and this man is off like somebody yelled FRESH BATCH.

Here's what the text says. When Abraham saw the men, he ran from the entrance of his tent to meet them and bowed low to the ground (Genesis 18:2). He didn't wait for them to walk up. He went to them, and he went fast.

Water first, friend. Abraham says, “Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree.” (Genesis 18:4). Travelers in the heat would want that, I bet. Offering a rest and a wash before anything else is a warm way to say welcome.

Oil on the head sounds fancy, friend, like a spa day under the oaks. But oil isn't in Abraham's offer. He says, “Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree.” (Genesis 18:4). Water for washing and a tree to rest under. That's what he puts on the table first.

explanations.answer: Robes to wear in the shade
explanations.explanation: Robes! Abraham is running a tent, not a department store, friend. His offer is simple: “Let a little water be brought, that you may wash your feet and rest yourselves under the tree.” (Genesis 18:4). I think a cool wash and some shade were all those travelers needed in the heat of the day.

Bread, friend. Abraham says, “And I will bring a bit of bread so that you may refresh yourselves.” (Genesis 18:5). Notice he calls it a bit. Hold on to that word, because this meal gets a lot bigger as the passage goes on.
Fruit isn't in his offer. Abraham says he will bring “…a bit of bread so that you may refresh yourselves.” (Genesis 18:5). Bread is the word he uses. Fruit doesn't come up at all in this meal.

Honey! Okay, I see you, baker. You're thinking like somebody who has stood in front of a cooling rack. But Abraham says, “And I will bring a bit of bread so that you may refresh yourselves.” (Genesis 18:5). Bread is the word he uses, and he even calls it a bit. Hold on to that word, because this meal is about to grow.

A tender and choice calf is what he picks. Genesis 18:7 says Abraham ran to the herd, selected one, and gave it to a servant, who hurried to prepare it. Remember he only promised a bit of bread. Now there's a whole calf involved, and I think Abraham is just getting started.

explanations.answer: A young goat from the flock
explanations.explanation: A goat is a good guess, friend, but look where Abraham runs. He runs to the herd, and the herd means cattle. There he selects a tender and choice calf (Genesis 18:7). A man who promised a bit of bread is now picking out a whole calf. I think his guests are about to get way more than they ordered.

That ram belongs to a later story, friend. In Genesis 22:13, Abraham sees a ram caught in a thicket by its horns and offers it up as a burnt offering. Here at his tent, he runs to the herd and selects a tender and choice calf (Genesis 18:7).

Close, but that's not what the text says. Genesis 18:8 says Abraham set the food before the men and stood by them under the tree as they ate. He's standing, not sitting. I think a man who just ran around fixing a feast might not want to stop moving.

False is right. Abraham brought the curds, the milk and the prepared calf, set them before the men, and stood by them under the tree as they ate (Genesis 18:8). He serves and he stays close. The text never has him sit down to eat.

That's the question, friend. “Where is your wife Sarah?” they asked, and Abraham answered, “There, in the tent…” (Genesis 18:9). They ask about Sarah by name. I think that question is worth noticing, because of what comes next.

Ishmael is Abraham's son, born to Hagar (Genesis 16:15), but nobody asks about him here. What the men ask is, “Where is your wife Sarah?” (Genesis 18:9). They ask about Sarah by name. Ishmael doesn't come up.

Eliezer of Damascus is a man Abraham once named as the heir of his house (Genesis 15:2), but he doesn't come up at this meal. The men ask, “Where is your wife Sarah?” (Genesis 18:9). Abraham answers, “There, in the tent…” The question is about Sarah, and it sets up everything that comes next.

True, and it's big news. The LORD says, “I will surely return to you at this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!” (Genesis 18:10). The promise comes with a time attached: this time next year. And Sarah is right there, listening at the entrance to the tent.

The text says the opposite, friend. In Genesis 18:10 the LORD says, “I will surely return to you at this time next year, and your wife Sarah will have a son!” The promise of a son is right there in His words. That's the heart of the whole visit.

She laughs, friend. Genesis 18:12 says, “So she laughed to herself…” She's been listening at the entrance to the tent and she hears this news (Genesis 18:10). I think a quiet laugh like that is hard to hold back when the news sounds impossible.

No tears in the text here. Genesis 18:12 says, “So she laughed to herself…” And she has words to go with it: “After I am worn out and my master is old, will I now have this pleasure?” That's a laugh and a question, friend, not a sob.

The text doesn't show her praying here. Genesis 18:12 says, “So she laughed to herself…” That's her reaction, and it stays inside, between her and herself. The very next verse has the LORD asking about that laugh (Genesis 18:13).
Abraham, friend. Genesis 18:13 says the LORD asked Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh…” Sarah laughed to herself, and the LORD still brings it up. Abraham is the one who gets the question.

Ishmael is Abraham's son, born to Hagar (Genesis 16:15), but the text doesn't mention him in this scene. Genesis 18:13 says the LORD asked Abraham why Sarah laughed. Abraham is the one the text names.
Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5), isn't named in this part of the story. The text says the LORD asked Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh…” (Genesis 18:13). Abraham is the one who gets asked.

explanations.answer: Nothing is too difficult for the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the point, friend. The LORD asks, “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). Then He repeats the promise: He will return at the appointed time, and Sarah will have a son. Sarah heard something that sounded impossible, and He answers it with that question.

explanations.answer: Sarah should not listen at the tent
explanations.explanation: The text says Sarah was behind Abraham, listening at the entrance to the tent (Genesis 18:10), but the question isn't about that. The LORD asks, “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). He's talking about what He can do, and then He promises a son again.

explanations.answer: Abraham should have told her sooner
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text points there, friend. The LORD asks, “Is anything too difficult for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). The question is about what He can do. Then He says again that Sarah will have a son at the appointed time.
Right, she says it. Genesis 18:15 tells us Sarah was afraid, so she denied it and said, “I did not laugh.” I think anybody caught like that would grab for a quick answer.

That's not what she says. The text says Sarah was afraid, so she denied it and said, “I did not laugh.” (Genesis 18:15). She talks about the laughing. Nothing in the text has her saying she wasn't listening.
The text doesn't have her saying that. Genesis 18:15 tells us Sarah was afraid, so she denied it and said, “I did not laugh.” She denies it. No apology comes out of her mouth in this verse.

True, friend. The LORD replies, “No… but you did laugh.” (Genesis 18:15). He says it plainly, and nothing in the text shows Him raising His voice. Sarah said she didn't laugh, and He answers her right there.
The text says otherwise. When Sarah says, “I did not laugh.” the LORD replies, “No, but you did laugh.” (Genesis 18:15). He doesn't let her denial stand. The answer comes right back to her.
